utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are some procedural matters to deal with first of all. Mr. Nice, I'm going to first of all give a ruling on the 92 bis applications for the next ten witnesses to hear argument about that. The Trial Chamber also wants to raise the question of the latest witness list. There is then the question of the Rule 70 applications and the issue as to Mr. Vllasi's evidence, all of which needs to be dealt with. I understand there is not unusually some pressure of time today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think these matters which have simply got to be dealt with can mostly be dealt will briefly and all serve the purposes of bringing efficiency to the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I turn then to the applications in relation to what were in the original list which I had, last week's list, the next ten witnesses who if was applied should be called under 92 bis. Mr. Thaqi Milazim, Draga Mustafa, Loshi Liri, Hoxha Hani, Haxhiavdi Ismet, Berisha Shyhrete, Gjogaj Ali, Berisha Halit, Berisha Hysni, Xhemajli Sadik. I read out the list as it appears on the Prosecutor's list. The Trial Chamber has had the opportunity of considering those statements. They are all witnesses who go towards the crimes themselves. None of them relate to the acts or conduct of the accused. They are all cumulative and therefore subject to any submissions which are made. They are admissible under Rule 92 bis. Technically, the accused has the right to be heard on these matters. Mr. Milosevic, is there anything you want to say? We shall order in each case the witness shall be cross-examined unless you indicate that you would be prepared to forego cross-examination in any particular case. Is there anything you want to say about our ruling or as to why we shouldn't make the ruling?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know my position, that is to say that I object to this en masse use of Rule 92 bis, because it limits the possibility for cross-examination. I don't think that in any trial this rule is applied as massively as it is here, and everywhere else witnesses are heard for several days. It is only my time for cross-examination that is limited to 45 minutes or thereabouts. So I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We've considered the matter of cross-examination and the length of it. We've considered is it in light of all the other considerations in this trial. It is not a relevant matter as far as whether these statements should be admitted. They will all be admitted under Rule 92 bis. Mr. Nice, I turn next to deal with the latest Prosecution witness list. The -- if I may deal with it first in the comment. The number of witnesses to date called is 78, by my calculation. The new list which has appeared today does not contain numbers. We have asked that in future, witness lists contain numbers. Not only is it important for those who have to deal with the list, it also would bring home, perhaps, to those calling the witnesses the sheer number involved. On that list, there are 72 names. One we have heard, Mr. Walker. One is to be recalled, Dr. Baccard. But if leave were given for all 70 witnesses, as it would be, the total for Kosovo would be 148 witnesses. The original order was for 90 witnesses. An application to vary was made on the 2nd of May, when 41 witnesses had been called before that, and the application was to call a further 95, a total of 136. Mr. Nice, what is of concern to the Trial Chamber is that far from there being a reduction, we're now in the position of an increase in witnesses. It's gone up rather than down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I explain? I'm sorry that the list alarmed you. Far from it being intended to alarm you, it was indeed intended to console you and cheer you, for reasons that I'll come to. As to the -- I know we're dealing with these matters more fully next week, but the reason I wanted to get this list in now, I'll come to in a second. But in fact, what the Prosecution has done - apart from eliminating further names from its previous list, as we'll see, and maybe including lists that cover both Kosovo and other parts of the indictment in this list - what we have done, as we will demonstrate next week, is get remarkably close to or very close to the deadline that was imposed, without prejudice to our arguments about the appropriateness of that deadline or the need for some additional time. But we've calculated - and we'll show you this more particularly next week - that if we follow Your Honour's observations on the last time this was discussed and, in general, take witnesses that deal with more than one part of the indictment later rather than earlier, we get actually very close to the 26th of July. But that can be achieved, first of all, with some flexibility - and I'll explain what I mean by that and why I thought it helpful to serve this witness list annotated in the way it is now - and may also require some reconsideration of some of the 92 bis witnesses. As to flexibility, we are pretty nearly going to come to the end of crime-base evidence by the end of next week. There will be one or two things outstanding, but not much. It's only because we've had crime-base witnesses waiting that we've been able to keep your days full of evidence, which is absolutely essential when time is limited. When we move away from having a reservoir of crime-base witnesses, it's going to be more difficult to make the best use of time, and so we've had to give some thought to how we can best be certain not to lose time. If you'd be good enough to go to page 4 - this is one of the reasons for serving the document this week, ahead of the weekend, so the accused and others can plan - you'll see that two witnesses who are available because they work here, Coo and Torkildsen, have been moved up, subject to my leaves that may be required, but with a view to being called at roughly those points in the witness list. Because we can foresee, doing what we can by way of putting witnesses against days in the calendar, we can see the possibility of gaps occurring there, and therefore, we would ask that consideration be given to preparing those witnesses in time for them to be called about them, should a suitable gap appear or should it be appropriate to hear them then. The next aspect of flex --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'll just ask: Is the financial expert's evidence, Torkildsen, is his evidence related exclusively to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not. It's very substantially to Kosovo. So, I mean, there's always the chance of taking him outside. Our judgement was that it would probably be more helpful to have him here. We can reconsider that and take him in the latter part of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If I may interrupt. I think, speaking for myself, that it would be helpful to have the broader witnesses later, when one has seen the full extent of the trial, and therefore the Trial Chamber will have the issues before it, rather than earlier, where it may be difficult immediately to see the significance of particular parts of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's a very helpful amplification of Your Honour's earlier remarks. We'll bear it in mind, and we may review the position so far as Torkildsen is concerned. Coo is pretty well specific to this part of the trial, so the same considerations don't apply to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pausing there, it may be helpful if I make this observation: that we've had from the amicus some objections to part of Mr. Coo's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These deal with the witness making conclusions, which it appears, certainly at first glance, not appropriate for the witness. If you look at the amicus's response, you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've reviewed it, but not recently, and I think, in fact, a large number of them can be met by considerations of the text. I think it's the materials that constitute the conclusions rather than the witness. But we have that point in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next aspect of possible flexibility that we've identified in this list is in respect of 92 bis witnesses, and it occurs to us that there may be some whom the accused himself, because of their particular status, he might not wish to cross-examine. K31 on page 3 is certainly one of them. And there are other witnesses who, it occurs to us - we'll discuss this in more detail next week, with your leave - that it may be appropriate for the Chamber even to reconsider as to whether they really merit cross-examination. Because, of course, it's not open --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not just the accused saying that he requires or demands the rights of cross-examination. It is a matter for the Chamber. And so in the interests of shortening the duration of this part of the trial, we're going to ask you next week to consider that as a possibility for a number of witnesses, not that many, but for a number, and depending on the outcome of that, we'll have to make such further decisions in respect to some of those witnesses as we think appropriate. But this is all aimed at shortening things in a responsible way. And I should say that lest there be any doubt about it, right from the beginning we've been concerned to conduct this trial, and all parts of this trial, in the shortest proper period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, having heard you, and speaking for myself, I think that is sufficient for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But I do reiterate our order, so there's no mistake about it: 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we quite understand that. The Court knows that my last application was for a necessary extension. May I simply say that I think you will be heartened to discover how close we can get to that without the need for an application. There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just make two points, because I think they're important. Although there are understandable and good reasons for taking witnesses who cover more than one part of the indictment later rather than earlier - and of course, to take such witnesses earlier rather than later might be to put us in difficulties with meeting the 26th of July deadline - there may be one or two witnesses whom it is very important to take early, either because of their own personal positions or because of the effect that their giving evidence may have on others. And I'll return to that topic next week. The second thing is that getting near to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who are those two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: K33 is one of them, and he's down for three days. And I think the Chamber may have had an application in respect of him covering his pseudonym. Now, perhaps I can say a little more about that next week, but one can imagine -- in the trial, we've already seen a change in the attitude -- we've seen a change in the attitude of witnesses coming to this Tribunal to give evidence, and it's a slowly developing and very welcome change. It needs every encouragement it can get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next topic - I can perhaps move more swiftly -- oh, no. Getting near to the 26th of July deadline does not allow for the remaining Rule 70 witnesses who remain unnamed in the list. As I indicated on the earlier occasion, A, I can't say anything about them; and, B, if they were to be available and if the Chamber decided it wanted to hear them, as it very well might, they would take some time. But that's an issue that's going to fall for resolution, if at all, later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should deal with one application for two extra witnesses which you've made. We will allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vlassi, can I deal with him briefly? You've had an opportunity to see Vlassi's brief statement, and we've reviewed the position overnight. Vllasi is a person able to give detailed evidence from great proximity to this accused at a time that is material in the development of the history, but it occurs to us that valuable though he would be in the Kosovo segment, he may be more appropriate as a witness in respect of the case as a whole, if at all, and so what we are going to do is to put back our application for leave to call him until a later part of the trial, the need being added to the other list, but we've given early notice, and we will revert to that matter later. Can I then turn to Dr. Baccard? We would like to be able to call him to deal with one outstanding issue next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We give leave for him to be recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. General Naumann. The Court gave an indication of its approach to General Naumann's testimony. He's here, ready to go today. His summary in English, signed, was disclosed on the 3rd of May and a signed version of his proofing summary on the 30th of May. These were, in each case , the earliest possible dates that they could have been served, General Naumann having been a witness whose status vis-a-vis Rule 70 may have been ambiguous to begin with, and as soon as those ambiguities were resolved, his statement was served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we gave leave to call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Effectively, Your Honour. I understood it to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- thus. The Chamber has issued a Scheduling Order in respect of the Croatia-Bosnia part of the case for return next Thursday. I think I've already told the Chamber that for our discussions next week about witness lists, I'm anxious to be able to provide you with a combined Croatia-Bosnia order of witnesses, and my intention is that I shall be able to provide you with a reasonably certain list of witnesses to cover the first three or four months of that segment of the trial. And included in my reasons for wishing to do that is to ensure that the accused, who makes observations about the amount of material served on him, shall be able to identify what work needs to be done by himself and by his associates as soon as possible and certainly in the course of any summer break. So we hope to have that list available next week as part of the general material to guide the Chamber as to how the trial's going to develop. As for the Scheduling Order, you will see my learned friend Mr. Groome here, he, as you know, having particular responsibility for the Bosnia part. And we hope that you will be heartened to know that of the 47 municipalities originally indicted, nine have been eliminated altogether. The proposal is to deal in full with 14, of which eight, it is hoped, can be dealt with fully by 92 bis, leaving only six municipalities to be proved in full. As to the remaining 24, there is an intention further to reduce the material in order to focus simply on the best and most important pieces of evidence from those 24. That exercise, it may be difficult to complete by next Thursday, and therefore, although we will respond fully to your Scheduling Order by next Thursday insofar as we can, we may find difficulties in reflecting the proposed further reductions of those 24 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That brings me to the Rule 70 issue. I would ask that I be allowed to deal with this in private session because of the sensitivities of the government concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, we've heard you firmly on these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it? What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Nice explained that I could, during the summer recess, familiarise myself sufficiently with the documents and material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to come back to that. We have to deal next week with the next part of the case. When we deal with that, we will consider what time is proper for you to have for preparation. All that's going to be resolved next week. It's not going to be resolved now. Now, we need to get on with calling the witnesses. We need to call one witness, anyway, or start one witness. Mr. Nice, you can help us with this. We adjourn, I guess, at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The plan was to call a crime base witness followed by General Naumann. I've rather eaten into the time. It might be desirable to take General Naumann first, but I know that my learned friend Mr. Ryneveld, who is calling him, wishes to have I don't know how many minutes with him first, and of course, a crime base witness can take up to an hour and typically does. A possibility would be a short, early break, but then of course that imposes on the interpreters to go beyond an hour and a half in the second session, unless for any reason the Court wanted to arise early for the short adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with this: General Naumann is anticipated to take how long in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I intend to lead him through the statement that has been disclosed, and I think I should probably take a session and a half in chief. He has -- I'm sorry. He has arrived during this session, so I've not had a chance to speak to him since April, as it were, and I need a couple of minutes just to ensure that matters will go smoothly in court rather than try to do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's available tomorrow; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. He's made himself available for the balance of today and all of tomorrow, but I understand we have a short day tomorrow in the sense that we don't go to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I recollect, it's 9.00 until 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's correct. So as long as he can complete by then that's fine. And I think rather than call a crime base witness and start and wrap around, it might be prudent if we start General Naumann forthwith. But as I say, I'd have to ask for the Court's indulgence for a short period of time just to ensure that everything's ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take the break now until ten past eleven. We'll then start again. We may go on a little longer, with the indulgence of the interpreters. Not too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Numbered witness lists now available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until ten past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I commence, I should advise the Court that General Naumann has kindly consented to come to testify. He was a Rule 70 witness for whom consent has been given. He is aware of the conditions of Rule 70(C) and (D), and if necessary, is aware of the fact that if there are any questions which go into the issue of confidentiality, that he may invoke those personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We may be concerned about the implementation of Rule 70 and whether and how it applies in this particular case, but it would seem the sensible thing is to hear the evidence in chief and then consider Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honours, that the issue will not arise. I just wanted to alert the Court before the issue...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld. There is an initial hurdle that has to be overcome by the Prosecution in relation to Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is in paragraph (B). I think it's entirely a matter for the Chamber to be satisfied that the Prosecutor is in possession of information that has been provided to it on a confidential basis, and that that information has been used solely for the purpose of generating new evidence. All of the other provisions in Rule 70 flow from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: From (B). That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From (B). So that is why I was a little concerned when you said that evidence is being given on the basis of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It is perhaps more accurate to note that permission had to be sought for this witnesses to give evidence. That permission was granted. The witness is prepared to testify in accordance with what is in his statement, what has been disclosed. My understanding is that there may be some areas that go beyond the scope of his statement, for which the witness may seek to invoke confidentiality aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Really, it's an issue of confidentiality --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- rather than Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's hear the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: General Naumann, sir, I understand that you joined the German Bundeswehr in 1958 and you were trained and held a variety of command and operational positions. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you were ultimately promoted to the rank of Brigadier General. What year was that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was in 1986, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And then in 1991, were you further promoted?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I was repeatedly promoted, but in 1991 I was promoted to the rank of four-star General.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, did you hold any position with NATO?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, I held positions with NATO before my promotion to the rank of Brigadier General, as a Colonel, and then in 1994 I was elected to be the chairman of the NATO Military Committee, and I assumed my duties as NATO's highest-ranking military officer on the 14th of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how long, sir, did you serve in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I served until the 6th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your role as chairman of the Military Committee, I understand that you chaired a couple of committees. Could you very briefly describe what your role would have been as chairman?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, the role of the chairman of the Military Committee of NATO is to translate the guidance which the NATO council, in its various configurations, ranging from the Ambassadors' level through the defence and Foreign Ministers to the heads of state and government level, issues in two strategic directions to the two strategic commanders, Supreme Allied Commander Europe and Supreme Allied Commander Atlantic. And at the same time, the chairman of the Military Committee has to receive the requests, the proposals of these two strategic commanders, discuss them in the Military Committee and forward military advice to the council on all those matters which either nations or the strategic commanders wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to pause between your answers and my questions to allow for translation, because we both speak the same language here. General Naumann, in 1998 and 1999, were you, in the capacity you have described, concerned at all with matters of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, beginning of -- at the beginning of 1998, NATO became seriously involved in the Kosovo conflict, and in my capacity as chairman of the Military Committee, it was my duty to report on the evolution of the situation and also to translate political direction given by the council how to deal with the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In the course of your duties, sir -- I realise you had a number of duties, but I want to focus on these: Did you, in your capacity as chairman of the Military Committee, participate in meetings with the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: On three occasions I met with the president of the former Republic of Yugoslavia. That was the first time when I accompanied the Secretary-General of NATO, Mr. Solana, when he went to Belgrade. I think it was on the 15th of October, 1998. Then I went a second time together with General Clark, the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, to see inter alia Mr. Milosevic on the 24th and 25th of October, 1998. And we were sent a third time by the NATO council after the events in Racak on 19th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If we may deal with those three meetings, sir, in that order. I'd like you to focus your attention, first of all, to that first meeting on the 15th of October of 1998. Can you tell us what the purpose of that meeting was and how it was that it came about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The meeting came about after NATO saw with ever growing concern the events in Kosovo which led to a serious deterioration of the situation, I think best expressed by the fact that according to figures provided by the UNHCR, some 220.000 citizens, inhabitants of Kosovo, were sitting as refugees somewhere in the bushes and winter was imminent and the hostilities in Kosovo continued. And NATO was desperately seeking a way to stop hostilities and find ways for these people to go back to their villages and towns. To that end, NATO had discussed what possibilities one could have, short of the use of military force, and had decided that NATO should be ready to act, and to that end an activation order had been agreed upon by the 16 NATO nations. The Secretary-General of NATO, Javier Solana had been asked by the council to go to Belgrade to deliver a very strong, straightforward message to the president of the former Republic of Yugoslavia, to find ways to cease hostilities and to stop violence in Kosovo since it was the common view of all NATO nations that the events in this part of Europe really contained the risk that an entire region may be threatened in its stability and peace was in danger. And that was the mission of Mr. Solana, who went to Belgrade, was received by Mr. Milosevic, and he delivered this message. And Clark and I were more or less the military witnesses prepared to explain what the NATO message meant and what the demands were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I pause there to ask you, sir, you refer to an expression called an "activation order" that had been agreed upon by all 16 nations. What do you mean by an "activation order"?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We have in the NATO military parlance -- and, Your Honour, I ask for your forgiving me that I use such an expression. In the NATO military parlance, we have three steps of preparing the forces for action. The first one is the activation warning, which means that forces of nations get a warning order to be prepared for military action. Then the next step is the activation request in which nations are requested to provide forces at a number which the nations have to decide upon and at a state of readiness which allows them to take action at rather short notice. And then they report back to NATO and tell NATO, "Our forces are ready for deployment." For instance, if forces have to be deployed from, let's say, overseas, from the United States or Canada, then they will presumably be deployed to forward bases in Europe if the theatre of operation is Europe. And the last step is the activation order, which means that the nations will issue the order to their forces which they have committed for such a NATO operation to execute military operations against a country or an alliance as authorised by the NATO council. And this means in many countries, for instance in my country, that the parliament has to take a decision on this activation order, since with that decision, activation order, the forces of all NATO countries have to be prepared to start military operations wherever it may be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do I understand your evidence to be, then, sir, that at that particular stage, approval from the various authorities of the representative countries had all been obtained and you had your activation order ready to be acted upon if and when required? Is that what I'm understanding? Please correct me.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. Your understanding is absolutely correct. And I may recall that Mr. Holbrooke had been in Belgrade to negotiate with Mr. Milosevic, not on behalf of NATO, but he acted as an American envoy. And he came back and reported to NATO that he may achieve an agreement, but he may need a last convincing argument, and that is the threat of NATO to undertake military actions, if necessary, if no agreement was possible. And when he gave this impression of his to the NATO council - if I remember correctly, it was on the 12th of October, 1998 - the NATO council, after deliberations and consultations with capitals, agreed, right in the middle of the night - quite unusual for Brussels habits - to declare the activation order, and with that NATO decision in his pocket, Mr. Holbrooke returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. I'm grateful to you for answering that sort of side issue, but I want to get back to the meeting of the 15th of October. And you've indicated, I believe, that there were a number of people from NATO that went. You referred to Solana and you referred to General Wesley Clark and of course yourself. When you met there, with whom did you meet? Do you recall, or would you require assistance from your notes or ...

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think -- I definitely remember that of course Mr. Milosevic was present, who welcomed us in the palace, in the White Palace of Belgrade. It was also General Perisic there, the then chief of General Staff, and Mr. Milutinovic. These are the ones I recall by memory. But if I had to read out the other names, I think I'd have to ask for the permission to look into the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to look at your notes, General, at any time, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Well, as I have stated in my written statement, it was there Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Perisic, a personal advisor to Mr. Milosevic, possibly Bojan Bugarcic; and on our side it was Mr. Solana, General Clark, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you've already told us, sir, about how the meeting came about. Were there any specifics discussed at that meeting? In other words, you've told us in general why NATO was concerned and what they had done in preparation, but at the meeting did you give any specific message, or were you present when a specific message was given to the accused, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, the specific message which Secretary-General Solana conveyed to Mr. Milosevic was that NATO was willing to act militarily if the violence in Kosovo was not stopped; if the military in feud positions, which was supporting the police, were not withdrawn to the barracks; and if the access deployment, which had taken place of special police forces, so-called MUP, and the military had been reduced to the normal peacetime posture. We also during this discussion presented some of the evidence which NATO had, based on intelligence sources, and in order to dispel the concerns which Mr. Milosevic raised that NATO's allegation were wrong and not based on the truth, precise data were presented to the Yugoslav side, and, inter alia, General Clark mentioned numbers of police units which we had seen acting in Kosovo and also army units which had been employed there, although they hadn't been garrisoned in Kosovo, and we did this by providing the numbers of these units. And I remember very well that Mr. Milosevic turned to the Chief of General Staff and asked him, "Are these forces there?" And after some reflection, General Perisic confirmed that the military forces we had mentioned were there and they were forces which are not garrisoned in Kosovo in peacetime, which do not belong to the Pristina Corps. They had been brought into Kosovo from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that General Perisic was confirming to Mr. Milosevic what you were alleging to be the case?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, one other question, sir. Were interpreters used during these meetings or were the proceedings conducted in English? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The conversation was entirely done in English. Of course, there were moments when Mr. Milosevic talked to his people, and using his mother tongue, but in all, interchanges between Mr. Milosevic, who did most of the speaking on the side of the Yugoslav authorities, and NATO, the language was English.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, in outlining these specifics, was there a general theme about the proportionality of force, for example, in these discussions?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, for us, the NATO side, the principle of proportionality is something which belongs more or less to our basic rules. We all are aware of situations that a country sees internal unrest, is confronted with terrorist attacks or something like this, and then it's our common understanding that a country has a right to defend itself against that. But if such a situation occurs, then of course the proportionality in reaction is more or less an iron rule. And I remember -- it was not on this event, but I remember - I think it was on the 24th, 25th October meeting - that I mentioned in the discussions we had to Mr. Milosevic and his advisors that my country, for instance, had also seen terrorist threats in the 1970s, when the Red Army faction really posed a serious terrorist threat to Germany, but we never had considered - and I think I mentioned this really literally - we never had considered the use of military force to cope with terrorism, and we never had considered to use military force or police force in a disproportionate way. So when we had a terrorist problem, we did never consider, even not in the wildest dreams of everyone, to surround the city by tanks and artillery and impound the city of the village first and then look after the terrorists after.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in some further detail when we get to the 24th, 25th of October meeting. In the meantime, sir, you've indicated to us that specifics were mentioned and that there was a discussion between General Perisic and the accused. Now, moving on, if I may, how long did this meeting last? When had it started and how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We arrived late in the afternoon, and the meeting ended up 10.00, 10.00 p.m. So all in all, I think some five hours or so. And I was present almost during the entire time. There was only a short moment when Mr. Solana asked for a one-on-one with Mr. Milosevic. And I know only from Mr. Solana's debrief what his general message was, and he told me later that this was a moment where he had really issued a rather stern warning to Mr. Milosevic to take NATO's preparedness to act serious and that this was the last chance to avoid hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there a particular reason why it was Mr. Milosevic that these warnings were given to? In other words, what was it about Mr. Milosevic's position that made you feel that he was the one to speak to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, he was the head of state of the country concerned. He was, as far as I know, the commander-in-chief of the military forces, and military forces were involved in the activities. And as head of state, he is also, I think, to some extent at least, responsible for what the police is doing. The police may be under the direct command of the Minister of the Interior, but nevertheless - at least, that's my understanding of responsibility - you can't carve it up at your liking. Responsibility for such actions is indivisible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is your understanding of his, if I want to use a legal phrase, de jure status. What was it, if anything, about the way in which Mr. Milosevic conducted himself at these meetings that led you to conclude he was the right person to talk to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, at all these meetings which I had with Mr. Milosevic, I had the impression that he was the man who was really in control of the situation. It was him who gave directions to our interlocutors, and it was him who had the final right to take a decision. And I think the most convincing episode to underline that, Your Honour, is on -- it happened on the 24th of October when we were in discussions with members of the police and of the General Staff in the building of the General Staff, and we had, after two or three hours of negotiating, we had not achieved too much. We had achieved - and it's also in my written evidence - we had achieved an agreement on a small, tiny area of Kosovo, but if we continued in that way, it was obvious that we would not achieve anything within the 48 hours which were given to us. And so we asked Mr. Perisic for a meeting with him. So Clark and I and a police general went to Perisic's office, and after Perisic had managed to get rid of the police officer, he told us, "If you want to achieve something, you have to seek another meeting with President Milosevic, since it's only him who can make the difference, and it's only him who can give the instructions." And from that I take that what I had said theoretically reflected also the practical reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Now, sir, you've already told us that about 10.00 or os the meeting was over, and I understand that the delegation then returned to Brussels, did it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We returned first to a hotel in Belgrade where Secretary-General Solana had a meeting with some press people. They were -- I think they were press people of press media or media who were not so much liked by the government. Some of them were opposition, clearly opposition. And that was a meeting in the -- in our hotel in Belgrade where Mr. Solana answered questions of these people and also declared the purpose of the visit. After that, we left and returned to Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not going to dwell on the details, sir, but you've already told us about being present on the 12th of October when Holbrooke obtained the activation order which you've described. Did you -- you were also in Brussels, I take it, when General Solana then briefed NATO about this visit you'd been on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you and General Wesley Clark obtain a tasking basically to do something after Mr. Holbrooke had established a framework for a formal agreement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: If you refer to the second task which we were given to go back to Belgrade on the 24th and 25th, yes, we got a tasking. Mr. Holbrooke had, if I may say so, achieved to -- to internationalise the Kosovo conflict, but he had not negotiated any details which led to a withdrawal of the forces which were there in excess of peacetime establishment. And the end of hostilities, the cessation of hostilities was not so obvious after Holbrooke's visit to Belgrade, and the signature of this Kosovo verification regime and -- that was the bilateral agreement between the Yugoslav authorities and SACEUR. But the withdrawal of forces was not settled. So the council, concerned that the situation may continue to deteriorate, decided to send General Clark and myself to Belgrade with the mission to find a way to reduce the forces. I'm using these words which may sound strange to you in order to avoid the word "negotiate," since at least one nation in the NATO council did have serious misgivings about sending generals to negotiate in something which they regarded as a political task. They had agreed and they had asked us, the military, to do this, but they didn't want to use the word "negotiate." And I think Mr. Milosevic will remember that we -- that we explained our, to some extent, awkward situation to him as well, that we are not there to negotiate, but the result we were supposed to achieve was the result of negotiation and was an agreement. So we went back with the aim to achieve an agreement which allowed NATO not to execute the activation order. So we wanted to find a peaceful solution which avoided the outbreak of hostilities between NATO and the former Republic of Yugoslavia. That was our aim. And with that intention, we came to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That brings us squarely to the October 24th and 25th meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's the purpose of the meeting, and that's how you got there.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. When you got there, what happened?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we arrived at the airport, were received by Ambassador Miles and the head of the KDOM mission - Kosovo Disengagement Observation Mission or something like that - Mr. Shaun Byrnes. They gave us a short briefing on the situation, and then we went to the White Palace and were received by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you say "we," were you accompanied by the US Ambassador Miles and Shaun Byrnes or it was just you and --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. They were with us when we went to the palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: And we also had, of course, a couple of collaborators with us. And we were -- one of them as -- and he was also present during most of the discussions. That was the Diplomatic Advisor to the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, Mr. Mike Durkee, an American citizen who is on NATO's payroll and is acting an a NATO employee, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was anyone tasked to take notes of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Durkee took notes, and he also produced, together with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. my personal staff officer, a German air force colonel, Gerhard Bischoff, they, together, produced on the way back, based on Durkee's notes, the report which we then gave to the NATO council in a written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. We've gotten a little ahead of ourselves but I just want to develop the structure. So on Saturday the 24th and Sunday the 25th, you then had these separate meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And who was present on behalf of the Yugoslav authorities?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, when we were welcomed by Mr. Milosevic, it was of course obviously himself; then General Perisic, the chief of the General Staff; the Deputy Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Mr. Sainovic, who was introduced as the one who is responsible for the Kosovo affairs; Mr. Milutinovic, I think the chief of the personal cabinet of Mr. Milosevic and the Foreign Affairs Advisor. Then later on we met with a couple of other military and police generals. This first meeting lasted approximately one and a half hours, and it more or less -- the aim was to set the scene and to explain for what reason we had been sent and what we wanted to achieve. It was followed by a meeting in which Mr. Milosevic was not present. It was done at the headquarters of the General Staff where we met with a couple of generals, colonels, officers, and where on our side also personnel of the KDOM mission was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to that, at this first hour and a half meeting, did you deliver a message to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. And I recall very much, very vividly, the words we used. I think the message we started with was that we said, "Mr. President, we came to deliver a very clear-cut, straightforward message. The hammer is cocked, the clock is ticking, and you have got 48 hours to deliver." That was the gist of the message. This straightforward, not very diplomatic language was not received with much enthusiasm, I should say, but it clearly set the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And were any specific details discussed in that initial hour and a half meeting, how to avoid the implementation of the activation order?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. We clearly stated that the key to everything was to reduce the military and police forces in Kosovo, to redeploy those forces who were in excess of peacetime establishment in Kosovo, and to cease the disproportionate use of force against civilian population. We also made very clear to Mr. Milosevic that we were only there to receive and obtain an answer to these demands and that we had to bring them back to the NATO council, that we were not entitled to enter any obligations for NATO with regard to the activation order. That was a decision to be taken by the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, once you delivered that message, sir, did Mr. Milosevic respond in any way?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall, Mr. Milosevic rejected the right of NATO to threaten his country with the use of force. He also rejected what he called our accusations, that the police and the military were using disproportionately force. He said that according to his knowledge, his police and his military acted in full concurrence with Serbian law, and he repeatedly denied that his forces, be it police or be it military, used tanks or artillery against villages and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is this when you told him the story about --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- your experience in your country?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I then took the -- mentioned an example which we had -- an information which we had gotten a couple of minutes before we had landed about an incident which had happened. According to the information we had, that the inner village was shelled. And Mr. Milosevic turned to Perisic and asked him whether he was aware of something like that. Perisic denied and said this did not happen. But of course, I would not -- neither blame Mr. Milosevic nor Mr. Perisic of not knowing something like this which had happened a couple of or perhaps hours ago. As we all know -- at least I know. And, Your Honour, you may not know it. I know how long it takes until an information is passed through the military chain of command and is really at the -- in the hands of the head of state or the head of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, as a result of that conversation which you say took about an hour and a half, did something else happen? In other words, were you directed to meet with other people? I believe you intimated that you did, later on, meet with other generals.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, at the -- after this exchange, this first exchange, and the explanation to Mr. Milosevic what our mission was all about, he directed his people to negotiate with us how we could come to an agreement, and we called it then, I think, technical discussions, to do this in the headquarters of the General Staff and to report back to him as soon as we had achieved a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that meeting, I take it, did take place later that same day, did it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That meeting began immediately after we drove down to the -- somewhere in Belgrade to the building of the General Staff. As I had intimated earlier on, we began with rather technical discussions with this huge delegation on the other side, did not achieve too much of progress. We concentrated first on an area, I think it was around the little town of Malisevo in Kosovo, and we discussed back and forth how -- what one could do to reduce tensions there and to find an agreement. It took us, I think, some two or three hours until we had found a more or less feasible solution for this tiny area. And we -- Clark and I, we came both to the conclusion it doesn't make sense to continue in that way since, otherwise, we would still be there when NATO was about to bomb. That would not have been a big problem for us, but otherwise, we would not achieve the aim to avoid hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You were concerned about the length of time these --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- the minutia of the discussions were taking?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We had -- we had 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Ah, I see.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: And within these 48 hours, we were supposed to achieve a tangible result that we could present to the NATO council so they did not take the decision to unleash the dogs of war. And for that reason, I think we pressed a little bit on time. And then we asked Perisic, as I had mentioned earlier on, what can we do to speed up the proceedings a little bit and really achieve a result. So Perisic advised us to go back and to see Mr. Milosevic, which we did, and the permission was granted to see the president a second time in the White Palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is this the incident you referred to earlier that if you really wanted to achieve something you had to speak to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. All right. So did you do that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We did do this, and we were -- Mr. Milosevic kindly agreed to see us a second time. So we went back to the White Palace, explained in -- I should say in a rather vivid exchange, if I may recall it properly, that it is now on the side of the Yugoslav authorities to turn the table and to reduce the forces, to withdraw them, to cease hostilities and to stop this disproportionate use of force. That was the content of the exchange which took place between Clark, myself, and Mr. Milosevic. And if I recall it properly, it was approximately after one and a half to two hours that Mr. Milosevic said that he wanted to consult with his close advisors. He went to a neighbouring room with them, and after a couple of minutes, perhaps half an hour, he came back and told us that he instructed them to negotiate with us with the aim to achieve an agreement. He also seconded Mr. Milutinovic to participate in these talks in the headquarters of the General Staff. And so we went back and began discussions, negotiations, which I think commenced around 11.00 in the evening and lasted until approximately something between -- I think we were in the hotel at 5.00 in the morning. But then we had a paper which both sides had accepted at referendum, and which both sides were prepared to present to Mr. Milosevic in the morning at 10.00 in the palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, sir, and just back up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's just a couple of details from paragraphs from 16 through 20. We've just sort of finished paragraph 20. We went very quickly over that. Just a couple of details that I'd like to return to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Without having you name the various individuals that were involved in these meetings in the technical discussions, sir, did you have any discussions about an appropriate figure during peacetime for MUP forces to be in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. We had a discussion, and I do not hesitate to inform the Court, Your Honour, that we, Clark and I, went to Belgrade with a number, which was 6.000, as peacetime strengths for the Kosovo police. That was violently denied by the Yugoslav authorities, and they told us - and they provided written information on that - that the number was 10.014, I think, approximately around 10.000. We had to admit that we may have good intelligence and reliable intelligence on military forces, where we can do based on information which you can obtain with overhead images, where you can calculate the strengths of military forces. You can't do those with police. And so after exchange of information, we agreed that we should accept the Yugoslav figure of 10.000, which meant that they had to reduce their police force which was in Kosovo at the point in time by about 5.000 to 6.000, within 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, the limited knowledge that you did have about MUP forces or police forces, did your intelligence sources basically tell you where some of these other police had come from? Were they all locals, or did you have information about where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We had, I think, fairly good information of where they came from and where their peacetime garrisons were. But what we did not have - and that was what I intimated to earlier on - is how strong such a police unit is, since some of them are sometimes doing their duties in civilian clothes, sometimes they're in uniform, and so it's much more difficult with military forces to come to a clear estimate how strong is such a police unit in terms of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, just reference to paragraph 19, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You've told us that as a result of this sort of private chat with Perisic, when he told you that if you wanted to achieve something, go speak to Milosevic, you did that, and this is now this two-hour meeting you talked about. Did you at that meeting discuss anything about the reduction of military and police? And if you've talked about that, I apologise. Just a little bit more detail. Did you actually say that to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, Your Honours, we clearly said to Mr. Milosevic that our aim is to bring the police force back to the peacetime strengths, the normal peacetime strengths in Kosovo, and that all military forces should be withdrawn from their field positions and should go back into garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were there, in the course of that discussion, any reference made to the KLA, or UCK?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. There was repeatedly, of course, made reference to the KLA, or UCK, when Mr. Milosevic described that they were taking action and that they were using force against Serb police forces, against Serb citizens, and that it was his duty, I think he said it in that way, to make sure that the country is defended against such people and that the citizens can live without -- free of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there a response?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, that brings us back, Your Honours, to the point we have discussed earlier on. I think we both said - and it also is reflected later on in the statement which we agreed upon - that of course a country has the right to defend itself against such -- against any terrorist threat, but the proportionality of defensive measures has to be observed, and that was not the case, according to our information and to our judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, as I understand the progression of things - please correct me if I'm wrong - after that meeting, he consulted with his advisors, came back, and said, "All right. Go away and negotiate." I'm paraphrasing this. And you hammered something out between 11.00 at night and 5.00 in the morning, and the deal then was to go back and meet with Milosevic the next morning at about 10.00, is that right, Sunday morning?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct. Sunday morning, at 10.00, in the Palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you pick it up from there, sir, as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we presented our results to Mr. Milosevic. He, I think, had read it, and he had also discussed it with his advisors, particularly with Milutinovic. It was another three-hour meeting. There were some details which were not liked by Mr. Milosevic, and there was also a certain problem on our side, since we had been very specific on the numbers of the police forces. But that was something which gave one country in NATO some difficulties, and so we negotiated some changes in that paper. And we called this agreement "statement." I think this paper is in the possession of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I might show this document to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, you can find it in Exhibit 94, and I believe it's tab 3. Perhaps, Mr. Usher ... Is that it? Thank you very much. Could you show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Tab 3, I'm sorry, of Exhibit 94. I think it's called "Record of meeting in Belgrade, 25th October 1998," and it bears ERN number 00766673.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. That's a paper which we agreed and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps, if you would, please, sir -- there are some signatures there, and perhaps you can tell us -- we'll actually deal with some of the document itself later, but the signatures, can you tell us how those appeared and some details of how they were placed there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, it was obvious that the paper had to be signed by those who had participated in the negotiations, and that was Mr. Sainovic, who signed it as the one who was responsible for everything in Kosovo; and it was also signed by Colonel General Djordjevic, who was at the time the Chief of Public Security of the Ministry of the Interior of the Federal Republic of Serbia. And then General Wesley Clark and myself signed the paper for the NATO military authorities. And we had some discussions with Mr. Milosevic whether he should sign this paper or not. Both of us, Clark and I, insisted that he should sign the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic asked the same question and was initially not inclined to do it, but we said to him, "We believe, Mr. President, that it is important that this agreement is signed by you, since without your authorisation, this paper will not have -- will not be fully respected in your country, and for that reason we ask you to sign it." After some lengthy discussions, Mr. Milosevic, if I may say so, grudgingly agreed to sign the paper and signed it, and that is the signature which you see on this paper without any printed name underneath it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just to an untrained eye -- do you know what kind of script or writing that's in, or is that ... Does that sort of look like a "C" with a dot and then the first thing looks like an "S" --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think the "C" with a dot stands for this Cyrillic "S."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Oh, it's Cyrillic. I see. Okay. So you're saying this line to the right of the two signatures, you watched it signed by --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I watched that Mr. Milosevic signed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, the document itself -- and the Court has it as an exhibit, and I don't want to take undue court time to go through it. But basically, sir, what does this document -- just if you were to summarise the effect of this document, what did you want it to show?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, the first page, which is the signed page, is simply a record of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: And we attached as an integral part of it this statement, which indicates what we negotiated, what the obligations were, which the Yugoslav authorities undertook in terms of bringing back excess forces to peacetime garrisons. It also spells out that the Yugoslav army will remain with some -- I think three company-size teams in field positions deployed to protect lines of communication, which are specifically mentioned in this document. It indicates at which point in time the withdrawal and redeployment will take place, and it provides for obligations which the Yugoslav side entered to inform KDOM and, later on, after deployment, an OSCE observer mission, to provide information so that they could also inspect the redeployed forces. And in addition, I think there's -- no. That was a separate statement. We have a separate agreement on the police behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Tab 4 of Exhibit 94. Might the witness be shown tab 4 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This is a document, sir, that is entitled, "Understanding between KDOM and Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia," and it bears number 00766672, and it's got a date 25 October 1998 on it. Is this the document to which you refer?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's exactly the document. And it contains what the police is allowed and obliged to do. It indicates that 27 observation points will be established along the lines of communication. The lines of communication are spelled out and the number of observation posts on these lines of communications is clearly indicated. It also spells out the obligations which the police forces entered. And the paper is signed by Mr. Djordjevic and Shaun Byrnes, the chief of the KDOM mission at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so we're clear and the Court has a clear description, was this document also then signed at that same time, or was that document already in hand? I realise it's the same day, but ...

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That document was in hand when we presented our work to Mr. Milosevic. And I have to add for the Court that this was presumably the piece of the paper which took us most time to negotiate, since we really were confronted with the attitude of the negotiating police officers, which wanted to more or less establish full and permanent control of every single, I should say, path in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So when you say there was a meeting from 11.00 to 5.00, did this document result from that lengthy --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It took us quite a time to get them to these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. But that document was available for Mr. Milosevic to read at the time he was asked to sign tab 3, Exhibit 94?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. All right, sir. You told us that he appeared somewhat reluctant but then did sign it. Was there a change in attitude at all after he signed the document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: After the document was signed, I think we saw a certain relaxation of the, to some extent, tense atmosphere we had had before that, and Mr. Milosevic kindly also offered us at this time I think a glass of slivovitz, and we talked a little bit more relaxed on what the future may bring. I think all of us had at this point in time the hope that this would lead to a reduction of hostilities and that we really would not be brought into the position to execute what we were sent to Belgrade to threaten Mr. Milosevic with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And during these discussions, sir, do you recall any particular statement that was made that you felt was of interest to the Court?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I recall one statement. And since I know that this statement has certainly some meaning, I double- and cross-checked it again with General Clark, who was also present. And I think, to the best of my recollection, Mr. Milosevic stated that he will try to find a solution for the Kosovo problem in spring of 1999. We had -- I should add for the information of the Court, Your Honours, that we had talked also about the proportion between the Serb Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. population and the non-Serb population, in particular, the Albanians, or Kosovars, and we had discovered that Mr. Milosevic and we had different numbers in our mind. He was always talking of a relationship which more or less meant that the approximately 900.000 Kosovar Albanians should be in Kosovo, and approximately 600.000 other nationalities, including Serbs. Our figures were considerably larger with regard to the Kosovar Albanians. In that context, he had also stated, and I think Sainovic as well, that one of the preconditions for a solution in the Kosovo area is to achieve a balance between the two ethnic groups. And he expressed -- or Sainovic, I think it was, expressed his concern that the reproduction rate of the Kosovar Albanians was much higher than of the Serbs, and that they had to find a solution which would not bring them back into the same problem within a couple of years. And in that context, it was talked about a solution in spring 1999. And we were wondering what he meant, and so we asked, "What do you mean with a solution?" And the answer was then, "We'll do the same what we did in Drenica in '45 or '46."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know what that was?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we didn't -- of course, we didn't know, and so we asked, and the answer was -- and that was a little bit -- well, it was difficult for us to take, but the answer was, "We got them together and we shot them."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who was present during that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Milutinovic. I think this advisor was the black beard. Mr. Milosevic would better know who it was. I think Bugarcic or something like that. The police general and Perisic. And on our side there was Clark and myself, and I believe also Mike Durkee was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, during that particular meeting of the 25th, and I'm talking a whole Sunday, did you form any impression about whether or not the accused was aware of what the Serb police were doing?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think in general he was presumably aware. I do not know whether he got all details. What they reported to him, in which detail, I simply don't know, but I left Belgrade with the impression that Mr. Milosevic was the man who was in control of the situation. Whether he knew all detail, whether he authorised all details, that, to the best of my knowledge, Your Honours, I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, in particular, referring to Exhibit 94, tab 4, the understanding where it details the relationship between the KDOM and the MUP, during the course of your discussions, did the accused seem to know about the details in that document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I'm really confident, Your Honours, that Mr. Milosevic was carefully briefed on the contents of this. And I also, as one of the reasons why I'm coming to that conclusion, I have to say that Mr. Milosevic repeatedly indicated that he is very concerned that the sovereignty of Serbia is fully respected. And what we agreed upon in this piece of paper means that a foreign authority, an international authority - in this case, for the first instance, the US KDOM, but later to be replaced by the Kosovo verification regime, KVM - would control Serb police forces and also, in the other agreement, Serb military forces, which is, for a man who was so concerned about national sovereignty, is clearly an infringement on national sovereignty. So I take from that that he was briefed on the details and that he agreed on these details as a way out for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've already told us that Mr. Sainovic had been introduced to you in a particular capacity by the accused Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct. And I can only repeat that he was introduced as a deputy prime minister and the man responsible for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General -- I'm sorry to interrupt you. When you heard from Milosevic that -- Mr. Milosevic, when he said, "We got them all together and shot them," how did you respond to those words? Did you try to clarify the words or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not. I think both of us were simply flabbergasted by that. We took it -- we couldn't -- we simply couldn't believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Turning now to paragraph 27, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: General Naumann, you've told us the purpose of the meeting, you hammered out these Exhibits 94, 3, and 4, and as a result of that, I take it, you recognised that by signature of that document, that the activation order would not have to be implemented; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we -- I think we had clearly said to Mr. Milosevic, Your Honours, that we had no authority to make any promises to that end. But I think we also indicated that we would recommend in our military capacity to the council to -- not to execute the activation order if this agreement was really met with full compliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. So you left the same day, Sunday, that afternoon, and went back to Brussels, did you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We went back to Brussels, went directly from the airport to Mr. Solana's residence where we met with Mr. Solana; the Deputy Secretary-General, Mr. Balanzino; and the head of the private office Mr. Domecq. We reported to them orally and undertook to provide a fully written report during the night for distribution to the NATO council. Before midnight of that Sunday the report was written, was circulated, and the next day the Secretary-General convened a council meeting where we had to amplify on our report orally and to share impressions with the council. And at the end of this council meeting on Monday, 22nd, the council came to the conclusion should the agreed withdrawal be fully implemented and should we get the respective confirmation by the people on the ground, the KDOM, then the activation order would not be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So subject to it being respected, the activation order was not acted upon.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. The activation order was put on the shelf. It remained dormant there as an instrument to be used should there be any violations. But on this very day, I think the NATO council was very pleased to see that there was a chance to avoid hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: As a result of that, to your knowledge were observations made as to whether or not this agreement was being complied with?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: To the very best of my knowledge, Your Honours, I have to say that the Yugoslav authorities honoured the agreement. They withdrew the forces according to this statement. That did not last for too long, I should say, but it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Initially, initially there was compliance.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: There was compliance, and I think one has to really pay tribute to what the Yugoslavs did. This was not an easy thing to bring 6.000 police officers back within 24 hours, but they managed. And I think we -- we all were very optimistic at the end of October that we had achieved a breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So as a result of your agreement that Mr. Milosevic signed, these things happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: These things happened. And I think that is a clear indication of what I had said earlier on. What Mr. Milosevic had decreed to do, it was done, and that was true in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did that last?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It did not last for too long a time. We saw -- as of November, we saw again and again reports of violations. I should really say, in all fairness, to the best information I got from the reports on the ground, from KDOM and later on from the Kosovo verification regime, many of the incidents were triggered by the UCK, who obviously tried to exploit the vacuum created by the withdrawn Serb security forces and who then sneaked in to take control of regions or areas. They also, I think, launched provocations, and they were not free of violence in doing that. The problem is that in many cases, as far as I have seen later on, particularly in the course of November and December, that the Serb side reacted again in a disproportionate way. It was, if I may say so, the old attitude to react to an incident where perhaps an individual had tried to kill or had killed a police officer, that they then again went in and used heavy weapons against villages and using disproportionately force against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And by December of 1998, had those reports caused you any further concern?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I had to report more or less permanently to the NATO council, and we had two concerns. First, that the entire regime was falling into pieces and that we were back in the spur of hostilities; and secondly, that we really lacked an instrument how to get the UCK or the KLA under control and how to influence them. We did not have an instrument to force them into compliance. And in addition, I have to say, Your Honours, we were not allowed. I, in my NATO capacity, I was never allowed to talk to any UCK man or representative since we had -- NATO had initially called these people terrorists. And the iron rule was that NATO will never negotiate with terrorists. That is also -- that's something which is not unimportant if you look at the composition of NATO, since in some NATO countries we have terrorist movements, and for that reason, these governments insisted that we should not talk to terrorists directly. With hindsight, it was perhaps a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But you complied with that directive, and you did not speak to any --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. I never spoke --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
