utterances.text: -- KLA?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I never spoke to any KLA man. I can assure you I never met anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you say, General, in hindsight it was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm asking why. Why do you say in hindsight it was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if you are in such a conflict, you should presumably talk to both sides and try to influence them to the best -- in the best possible way. Perhaps we could have -- we could have reduced difficulties in this area. Whether it would have led to -- to a peaceful solution, I cannot tell you, Your Honour. But I live with the conviction one should make every attempt possible to defuse a situation before one uses military force in order to enforce peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Having said that, sir, you've told us slightly earlier in your evidence that during one of your meetings with Milosevic and/or Sainovic, there was some discussion about -- I believe it was on the 25th of October there was this discussion about the Albanian Kosovar problem and some suggestion that that problem might repeat itself, and then you've discussed the comment that was made. Have you had an opportunity to reflect, sir, on what happened after December of 1998 in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we saw -- of course, after December we saw increased escalation. We saw increased violence, hostilities. We saw an increase of the numbers of refugees, and we -- we saw that more or less both sides tried to -- to expel people of the other ethnic group from the areas where they lived. That is definitely true for the Serb side, but it's also true to some extent for the Albanian side which also tried to get the Serbs out of the pockets where they clearly had the majority. And both sides, based on all the information we got from the OSCE mission, really had taken off their gloves and were using brutal force to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. That brings us, sir, to the 19th of January meeting. And before you do --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't have it clarified with you. Do you intend to go right to the normal time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We'll go just beyond quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. That gives me an idea. I'm about to start paragraph 30 on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us there were three meetings. The third meeting took place when?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The third meeting took place on the 19th of January, 1999, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And this is after Racak, I believe you said?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That is after Racak, yes. And Racak was the event which triggered the -- our dispatch to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Why did you go?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we were sent by NATO council to tell Mr. Milosevic that something like Racak was simply intolerable. I -- again, I do not hesitate to inform you, Your Honours, that both General Clark and I had done the utmost we could do ask the council not to send us, since we didn't regard the mission we were supposed to do as a military mission, and we thought we were the wrong people to do it. In contrast to the October meeting, we also did not have something which I would call a compelling argument for Mr. Milosevic since our stick, if I may say so, the threat with the activation order, had gotten a little bit weak and soft and was more a rubber baton than a stick. So we were not too happy to go, but we got the order. And for military officers, there is one thing which they have learned: They have to obey the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in compliance with that order you went and did what?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We went to tell Mr. Milosevic, I think in clear-cut words, that Racak and a repetition of Racak was simply unacceptable and could trigger military reaction. We also asked Mr. Milosevic to consider to give approval to Mrs. Arbour, who was sitting with the ICTY team in Skopje in Macedonia, to enter Kosovo and to visit the site of the events in Racak. And we also discussed with President Milosevic that the decision to declare Ambassador Walker to be a persona non grata in the country should be reconsidered and he should be allowed to remain in Yugoslavia. And of course, we also were there to invite Mr. Milosevic to return to the terms of the agreement we had had on the 25th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you say return to those terms, by this time did you feel that there was no longer compliance?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. There was no compliance. There was no compliance with regard to the police forces. There were more police forces in Kosovo at the time than agreed upon. And of course, and perhaps most importantly, the size of the army was far in excess, and also the use of force had returned to the disproportionality which had been one of the reasons for our negotiations in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't believe we indicated. Where did this meeting take place, and tell us what happened perhaps in stages. You've given us the points. Perhaps you can talk about Racak first. But first of all, where did this meeting take place and who was present?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The meeting took place in the White Palace in Belgrade. Mr. Sainovic, I think, was present. I think also the foreign secretary was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date was the 19th of January, 1999, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And -- well, you told us that one of the subjects was Racak. Did you discuss Racak with the accused, and if so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We discussed Racak. We had -- on the way to the palace, we had stopped with Ambassador Walker and received his report on the situation, what he had seen on the site. And we shared the observations of Ambassador Walker with President Milosevic, ending with the conclusion that based on that, we had every reason to believe that these people were not killed in combat, as had been alleged by the Yugoslav side, but that they had been shot after some incident had taken place there and that after all, they were civilians, and one of them was a 14-year-old boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you put that allegation to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and it was clearly rejected. Mr. Milosevic got angry when we mentioned this, and he -- he clearly told us that Serb police and military would never do anything which is against Serb law. He -- he accused us of having -- more or less having fallen or taken -- fallen into the trap of Mr. Walker's accusations, which had led to the declaration of him being a persona non grata, and that we took sides with Walker and that we made outrageous statements on this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you, General, as a military commander, did you make any observations of what you'd heard about the injuries to the accused?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We had -- Walker had shown us some photographs of these killed people, and I -- I think I -- I said to Mr. Milosevic that I could not imagine that anyone who can think of an infantry operation, that he could see the victims of such an operation with the wounds which were clearly visible on these photographs since most of them had shots in the neck. And you clearly could see that -- that this is not the way in which you kill people in an infantry operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How would -- how are soldiers trained to --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, to shoot someone in the neck means, first of all, that the person you are fighting has to turn his back to you. That's normally not the attitude you have when you are fighting someone. That's the way how someone is behaving when he is caught and then you can -- can do it, if you do not obey to the law of war. And secondly, if -- if one is fighting people in combat, most of the wounds will be somewhere in the upper body or in the head area and not in the neck and in the back. And we -- I think I can tell the Court that I have very often in exercises myself fired at targets. I do not -- I do not -- I do not remember a single event where even in an exercise one came into a situation where one could shoot into the neck of someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, you told us that Mr. Milosevic got angry. And how were you able to judge that he was angry?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, occasionally he got a little bit louder so that our people who were sitting in the anteroom watching those nice paintings which they have in the White Palace of Belgrade, that they got aware of that and were preparing for departure since they thought that we were about to be thrown out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did the topic then turn to Judge Arbour?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. That was the next issue we discussed. We tried to convince Mr. Milosevic that he should allow Judge Arbour to enter the country and to visit the site. As I have indicated in my written statement, there was no way in, and all formulas which we proposed were rejected. And of course, Mrs. Arbour, whom we telephoned in Skopje - General Clark did this using his cellular phone - did not accept anything which was less than unrestricted access to the site. And from an investigator's point of view, I think she was correct in doing this, since otherwise you can never come to a clear-cut judgement what happened at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, I take it there was some negotiations, but a stalemate, I take it, eventually was reached or -- I don't want to paraphrase here. What was the ultimate conclusion? Did a Finnish team eventually have access?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but -- that's correct. The finish term got later on access, and I think many of you, and in particular, Your Honours, you may have read the statement of Mrs. Ranta, I think was the name of the Finnish doctor. She, as far as I recall, made a public statement on the 17th of March, 1999, after she had conducted some autopsies, and she clearly came to the conclusion that these people were not killed in combat, and we provided detailed evidence for that so that the -- that there is still reason to believe that Racak was not a combat event but was the site of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, at the time these discussions were taking place, do you know whether or not, as negotiations to call in a Finnish team were taking place, whether or not autopsies had already commenced?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: As far as I know. But I have to say, Your Honours, I'm basing that on public information. I have no detailed and specific information that Yugoslav authorities had begun to conduct autopsies before this international team had access to the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I should clarify, General Naumann, in fairness to you. I'm not asking you to give us this evidence for the truth of it but whether or not that was information that you received that you then put to the accused and his reaction to it.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We mentioned that we had heard this and that this made it very difficult for an independent investigation to come to conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that was put to the accused by you or Clark?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It was put to Mr. Milosevic by either me or General Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And his response?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, he did not accept the argument. And since -- and I think, as far as I recall, this came back to the question of national sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You also mentioned, sir, that Mr. Walker's status as persona non grata was the subject of discussion, and I think you've mentioned to us that's as a result of what he had said about Racak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. That was our impression, that the decision was taken after Walker had made public statements on his impression on the events in Racak. And we tried, and I think -- yes, I did this. I tried to convey to Mr. Milosevic the impression that a country like Yugoslavia should not expel, more or less, an OSCE Head of Mission without having consulted with the head of or with the chair of the OSCE, which was at the time Mr. Vollebaek, the then Foreign Minister of Norway. And we also made the point that it would be good if Mr. Milosevic could agree to receive Minister Vollebaek, who was due to travel in his OSCE capacity to Belgrade. President Milosevic indicated that he was not willing to reconsider his attitude towards Mr. Walker since he had made incorrect and insulting statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So was the matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ryneveld. I'd like to get back to the word before it disappears from the transcript. General, you said that Racak was not a "combat event." Did you know that there was some -- there was a unit, KLA unit, in the village of Racak and there was combat and some KLA members were killed at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that in the entire event approximately some -- as far as I know, some 45 people were involved. Seven of them obviously were KLL -- KLA that were killed. But the people who were found in this trench or what it was, were obviously not KLA. They were unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And what you -- that is not far-fetched, Your Honour, since if you undertake an autopsy of someone who fought in combat, you will find traces of black powder on the hands if he had used a weapon, and Mrs. Ranta clearly stated that none of the victims had any traces of black powder on their skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time. Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When did you come to know the fact that there were KLA members among the people killed there at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we talked to Mr. Walker on this event, we asked him, "Did anything take place like a combat, a skirmish, between the KLA and the Yugoslav forces?" And he said that there had been an incident in this area, that some exchange of fire had taken place, but then in the -- in the often-described disproportionate use of force they had -- the Yugoslav security forces had entered the village and, according to what he had learned, got the people together and started to separate them or to take prisoners or whatever you, and some of them were obviously killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Following up on that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The conversation you had with Mr. Walker was on the 19th of January, upon your arrival, or earlier?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. It was on the 19th of January. We went to the embassy and got the information there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to start with paragraph 35. Did you wish me to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a convenient time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn for an hour and a half. General, would you remember, please, I must give you the formal warning since you're giving evidence, not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include the Prosecution team. Would you be back, please, at 2.25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: General Naumann, just before the lunch break, you had been telling us about the discussions you had with the accused on the 19th of January, 1999. You had earlier told us about four points, and I think we got to the fourth point, which had to do with the perceived non-compliance with the October 25th agreement. Can you tell us at this time, sir, what the particular issues were that were discussed on the 19th of January in that respect?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we discussed the excess number of police officers who obviously had been brought back into the Kosovo area; we discussed the non-compliance in terms of disproportionate use of force by police forces, as well as by military forces; and also the fact that armoured units were not in the garrisons, as it was agreed upon in the statement which we discussed earlier on here in these court proceedings. And in order to substantiate our claim of violations, we handed over a list of I believe ten incidents where we believe that the Serb security forces really had grossly violated the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And can you describe, if you would, please, how the accused responded to your indicating that there was non-compliance and providing him with details of the non-compliance?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, our accusations or allegations were not accepted, we never got a reply to the list which we had handed over, and our statement was rejected by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In particular, about disproportionate use of force?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: In particular that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there any comment about increase in troop movements or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, not from Mr. Milosevic's side. From our side, we indicated that we had seen increased troop movements outside Kosovo, which were referred to as winter manoeuvres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And can you describe for us, if you would, please -- do you know what he meant by "winter manoeuvres"?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, I think that is what everyone understands with that, that all military forces used to train occasionally, and when there were winter manoeuvres, winter exercises was used, we knew that the forces were out of the garrison, doing military exercises, routine exercises. The unfortunate connotation was that it was -- that these exercises took place so closely to the Kosovo area, and that with the deployment of the forces into the field, of course reaction time for an eventual deployment into Kosovo was shorter than if they had been in garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Now, when you provided this list, what was Mr. Milosevic's response, if any?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, the usual polite response: We'll look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you in fact subsequently get anything back from the accused --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- concerning that list or --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No, we never got anything back, but presumably that is also due to the development of the situation and the evolution of the situation. As you know, soon thereafter, the Rambouillet/Paris process started, and so these incidents, I think, were more or less overtaken by the political events.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, how long was that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It was approximately, I think, seven hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And who was present in terms of the Yugoslav side?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It was, as I had stated earlier, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, the foreign minister, Jovanovic, and the gentleman whose name I always have difficulties to pronounce, I think Bugarcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you've earlier, sir, taken pains to explain to us that both you and General Clark were somewhat reluctant in order to take this task but that you did go out on orders and fulfil this. As part of what you were to do, did you deliver any kind of a warning?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we stated that NATO would not watch without action the ongoing escalation and the increase of violence and that Mr. Milosevic should not be under any illusion that NATO would not be prepared to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, after you had this meeting, I take it you prepared a report and went back to -- you went back to NATO and reported on this meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at some point you had handwritten notes, and those notes have been transcribed in your written statement, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Most of it. As you may have seen from my handwritten notes, there are some elements of assessment in it. We did not include assessment elements in our written reports to the council. We provided the factual information, what had happened, how far we had come, and we reported on our -- I should say on our impressions the assessment part in a verbal way to the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir. Are you able to share with the Court your impression of Mr. Milosevic during your meetings?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, in -- yes, I can, Your Honours. During this meeting, I had the impression that Mr. Milosevic was no longer, I should say, amenable to arguments from our side. He seemed to be set on a certain course, and he -- he did no longer accept our main argument which we had used in October that Yugoslavia should be a part of Europe, a respected part of Europe, and not a country which by its own behaviour puts itself outside the community of European nations. That argument did no longer fly during that meeting. Perhaps -- and that was also an impression which I had at the time. Mr. Milosevic was also disappointed that we on our side hadn't been able to, if I may say so, restrain the KLA. He certainly had hoped that in return for what he had done in complying with the 25 October agreement that the KLA would refrain from action, but perhaps his expectations had been higher than one could reasonably have had since it's always a -- is an evolution which goes much farther back than 1998. And he obviously saw no longer a chance to come to terms with the KLA in a way which we had expected he could consider them, namely, a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: As a result of your discussions with the accused, was it clear to you that the accused knew that there was a distinct risk that Yugoslavia would be bombed?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic knew that NATO had the capability to really inflict serious harm on Yugoslavia. I think he also learned from our -- from our interventions that there was a determination to act if necessary as a last resort, if everything else had failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Having -- sorry. Having made that clear to the accused, did he respond in any way?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall, he -- he angrily said to us on one occasion, "I know that NATO has the ability to destroy Yugoslavia." And if I recall it properly, he also accused us that if we contributed to that, that we would be killed here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did he express any concern?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, as I have said in my -- in my written statement, he said, "Well, you could do what you wish. I do not care." And I think that was another indication that he had given up on believing that we could find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, I believe you've told us earlier, General, that it was clear that you and General Clark wanted to negotiate or deal with or have meetings with the accused, Mr. Milosevic. You did so. Did you, after these meetings, deal with any other authorities of the FRY or the former FRY?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I never had any other contact with any other authority of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, that -- then the process was taken over by the so-called Contact Group. The Contract Group consisted of France, Britain, United States, Germany, Italy, and Russia. They took the crisis management over in this phase. NATO was not to form a part of that negotiations, and in my NATO capacity I had no access to the negotiations, and I had influence on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to draw on your experience as a military general, if I may, and looking in retrospect at what occurred in the spring of 1999, are you able to indicate from just your military experience whether what appears to have occurred in the aftermath of -- in March and April, et cetera, of 1999, whether or not that required any planning, and if so, whether it would -- what groups would have to have been involved in that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, looking at the scale, complexity, and magnitude of the operation which later on the Yugoslav forces carried out in Kosovo, it seems to me that such an operation cannot happen without careful preplanning and preparation. And if we had to do this in a NATO country on a national basis as Yugoslavia did it, it would require, I should say, preparation which may last three to four months or something like this. So the beginning, the decision, must have been taken, if they applied our standards, by the end of 1998. It was -- if you look at it, it was without any doubt a carefully planned and carefully executed operation which, by the way, started well before the first NATO bomb was dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier about in the discussion with the accused giving an example of how forces might be used in your own country of Germany to deal with terrorist groups. Are you aware of anything from General Perisic about the use of military forces for internal security action?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: In -- I had only one meeting with General Perisic and that was the one on 24, 25 October 1998. And in this discussion which General Clark and Perisic and I had, he gave us the impression that he did not want the Serb army to be committed and employed in operations against citizens of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you aware what happened to General Perisic subsequently? Did he remain in office?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. He was ousted. I think it was by -- somewhat in November or so 1998. But I recall as a statement of Perisic which may play a certain role, he told us that he is fully aware that NATO could destroy the Serbian army if NATO wishes to do so and that his interest is to preserve, as far as possible, the integrity of the Serbian army which he described, and I think that is a verbal quotation, as the only democratic institution in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Turning to paragraph 44, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with Mr. Milosevic about the military problem in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. During the discussion which we had, Mr. Milosevic stated his belief that the Yugoslav armed forces could destroy, annihilate, eliminate the KLA within a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And you've told us about three conversations you had. Do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you recall which one of these conversations -- which one of these three meetings that conversation may have taken place?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure whether it was the October or the January conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, at some point, sir, you're aware that the KVM withdrew from Kosovo, and what can you tell us about - from what you know in your military experience - about the type of tactics that were used after KVM withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, as long as the KVM was in place, we had the impression that the impact on the Serb security forces was to some extent a restraining impact. They did not want to give too much evidence of severe violence. When the KVM was withdrawn, we saw an increase of violence, and this restraining effect had gone. On the other hand -- and some of -- perhaps, Your Honours, you may accuse us, when you hear that: Why did you then insist on the withdrawal of the KVM? Our problem was that we had 1.400 or more unarmed people in the territory of Kosovo, and we simply did not want them to be hostages should there be a further escalation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you say "escalation" of violence, were you able to determine, from the information you had, as to what Serb forces were involved in this and to what degree?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, not in detail, sir, I have to say, since with the withdrawal of the KVM, of course, I should say, the detailed knowledge of what happened on the ground decreased to some extent. We then had to rely on technical intelligence. And as you may remember, the weather conditions in this part of the year 1999 were not too favourable in the beginning of March to allow us to follow with our technical gadgets the events on the ground as closely as we would have liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were you able to determine whether or not the VJ was involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Based on some intelligence, we came to the conclusion that the VJ was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How about the MUP?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The MUP was definitely involved. I think most of the actions were carried out initially by the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: From what you could see or determine, based on your military experience, was there any coordination between these two forces?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We had seen incidents where obviously the VJ had been ordered to hand over materiel to the MUP, which then the MUP used. I also came to the conclusion, when we looked at the entire picture which was unfolding, that the operations were coordinated and that the central command for these operations was somewhere in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, were you aware at all of any particular units or armies or corps that were involved?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We came to the conclusion that the VJ 3rd Army Corps, with the headquarters in Nis, was the coordination centre, but on the other hand, the command and support which was necessary to sustain such an operation I think required support from elsewhere. So it was not the 3rd Army alone. The chain of command was presumably somewhere -- the 52nd Corps, which was in Pristina, then running up to the 3rd Army in Nis, and from there to the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One final area, sir. There came a time, I take it, in March of 1999, that you're aware that Ambassador Holbrooke saw the accused, Milosevic, on one final occasion. And thereafter, were you present, sir, when he reported back?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I was present at the council meeting which followed thereafter. Ambassador Holbrooke had been sent to Belgrade after the Rambouillet/Paris process of negotiations had broken down, and that was a last attempt to avoid hostilities. And he reported back that Mr. Milosevic was not prepared to negotiate, which meant at the same time that the political, diplomatic options had all failed. And with that impression, shared with the NATO council, the NATO council discussed the situation and then eventually authorised the Secretary-General to execute the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And by executing the operation, are you talking about acting on the activation order?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, the activation order was in place. What I mean with "to execute the operation" was that the operation plans which had been presented to the NATO council for a limited air option, as well as for an air operation against the former Republic of Yugoslavia, were executed, and that was what I meant with "the execution order."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the cross-examination starts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Ryneveld, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. Just before cross-examination starts, I'm asking if perhaps the Court might consider reserving five minutes at the end of today for a somewhat urgent administrative matter to be discussed. I just thought I'd announce that now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just remind us, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Naumann, is it true what I'm going to read out to you now: [In English] "The attack on Yugoslavia constitutes the most brazen international aggression since the Nazis attacked Poland to prevent 'Polish atrocities' against Germans." "Polish atrocities" are under quotations. [Interpretation] Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I would violently disagree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the position of Walter J. Rockler [phoen], former Prosecutor, Nuremberg war crimes trial. On the 10th of May, 1999 was when it was given and when it was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...go into it. It's another opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked whether it was true, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You got the answer. It isn't. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, as a general of the German army, who has reached the topmost ranks and has a long career behind you, what do you think about the fact that your country, on three occasions in the twentieth century --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we don't want this -- we don't expect to hear these generalisations. They're quite irrelevant. We're dealing with events now in 1999 and 1998. Restrict your questions to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, please. Would you bear in mind the fact that the witness spoke about our discussions and arguments, and he even mentioned that I told him that NATO did not have the right to threaten Yugoslavia; and that he conveyed these threats, together with Clark; that those threats had a political background to them and that he spoke about that political background publicly, and indeed here too. I therefore do have the right to examine him with respect to the circumstances and the political background and positions from which he departs in his presentation, and you cannot restrict that right of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Most certainly we can. You will ask questions which are relevant to the evidence which this witness gave. Now, if you want to ask him about the meetings, you should do so, but broad historical questions are irrelevant. Now, ask questions, by all means, about his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is linked to his evidence and testimony, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on. Move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think it's very flattering for you to protect the witness in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He is not being protected. The only protection is that of the Court against its being abused by you. Now, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that within the former Yugoslavia, a support for the aggression in 1999 you found precisely in those forces in Kosovo which were on the side of Germany in World War II, fought on the side of Germany in World War II?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this? What's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is that we are discussing the highest representative of NATO to take the floor here so far, and he was the top most military functionary of Germany, which played the leading role in breaking up Yugoslavia and that is precisely the subject of what we're talking about here in this room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll stop there. The General can deal with that allegation since it may have some relevance. What is alleged is that Germany played the leading role in breaking up Yugoslavia. General, you've heard that allegation. Was it your motive to do anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can assure you, Your Honours, it was not a motive. I have heard these allegations repeatedly as a German citizen and as a German military. Mr. Milosevic may remember that Germany executed a huge degree of restraint when all these events in the former Yugoslavia started. We're talking here about the fourth war which Mr. Milosevic ordered his forces to unleash. In the first three, Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, Germany executed the utmost restraint. But when we saw at the end that no other way was possible to restore peace and stability in a region of Europe which is not too far away from Germany, then we joined the consensus in NATO. It was a difficult discussion in my country, Mr. Milosevic, very difficult. And I myself have very often stated, when I was still the Chief of Defence Germany, that Germany, due to what it did in World War II, for which it tried to really to draw consequences and conclusions -- I may remind perhaps this high court that Germany is presumably the only country in Europe which bans by constitution a war of aggression, and no German citizen has ever violated that constitutional ban. That is, I think, a clear consequence of what World War II meant. But we also came to the conclusion, and for that reason Germany participated in the end in the Kosovo operation, that sovereignty means that a head of state is not allowed to do to his citizens whatever he wishes to do, that sovereignty is a responsibility to protect the citizens and to make sure that they can live under the conditions of pursuit of happiness. And when we saw that there is a country in Europe which is not able to do this and willing to do this, we joined the consensus in NATO and participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, we've dealt enough with history. Let us deal with the witness's evidence. You were at the meetings, so you've got the opportunity to rebut what was said, if you want to, and ask the witness about it. He made one or two very serious allegations, and you should deal with them in your cross-examination, but there has been enough history now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will come to those accusations in due course, Mr. May, but may I deal first with what the witness has just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That was an answer to your allegation at the beginning. He was given an opportunity to answer it and now that has exhausted that topic. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago the witness said that I used my forces in wars in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, and because during those wars I was President of Serbia, I don't know what army it was that I had and what army Serbia had in the wars in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia, and I'd be very grateful if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Those are other matters subject to this trial at a later stage. They're not, for the moment, relevant. Now, let's move on. You don't need to stop to argue about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now nothing is relevant. Excellent, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, do you know what Germany chose the 6th of April, 1992 to recognise the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the day when Hitler bombed Belgrade in World War II?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Really, Mr. Milosevic, this kind of question is getting us nowhere. If you are suggesting that this witness is biased in some way, then you must put it clearly to the witness, but general allegations of that sort are of no assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is not an accusation of any kind. It is a question based on the fact that Germany did proclaim the recognition of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 6th of April, and on the 6th of April 1941 Hitler, without any intimation, bombed Belgrade and destroyed it. And I'm asking now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to permit this sort of accusation. If you can't cross-examine this witness properly about his evidence, then the cross-examination will be brought to a stop. Now, you know what evidence he gave, and you should be dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you forbidding me to question the witness about his positions, Mr. May, about his political --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anything that has to do with his public appearances and statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to cross-examine him about something he said in public, you can certainly do that, but let's move on to it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll start from that end, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, at that time you were inspector general of the Bundeswehr. That is actually the chief of the army, right, the inspector General of the Bundeswehr? In European Security Magazine dated 1995, volume number 1, page 8, you say: "Germany has been united since the 31st of August last year. It is free from occupation troops, and in this way fully sovereign for the first time since the days of Richelieu. For the first time in 300 years, we have the satisfaction of not being an object of external pressures either from the East or the West. In this way, our country has the possibility of acting politically rather than reacting and can put all of this on a firm basis in NATO and the European Union. This only enhances the responsibility of Germany." Mr. Naumann, what do you mean when you say that from the days of Richelieu up to 1994, that is to say at the time between 1914 and 1918, when you waged the First World War, and from 1933 until 1945 in the days of Hitler that Germany was denied the privilege of not being subjected to external pressures? So what is the novelty of this all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've already said that history is not relevant. Now, let's move on. Find something which he said about Yugoslavia and you can ask him about that or about these particular events we're dealing with in the trial. Of course you can ask about that. But irrelevant matter just wastes the time of the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you not wish to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. What the position of Germany between Richelieu and 1914 or whenever it is is totally irrelevant. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And -- all right. Is this question relevant, Mr. May? In the light of what I've just quoted, I would like to ask Mr. Naumann why the borders in the Balkans now, with smaller variations, are the same as they were in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, you haven't answered -- General, I should say, you haven't had the chance to answer anything yet. Is there anything you can usefully say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, first of all, I think that Mr. Milosevic is -- is really to some extent confusing one issue. I was a German general serving NATO. I did not act on behalf of Germany. I acted on behalf of 16 sovereign nations of which Germany is one. And I think, Mr. Milosevic, I told you that on one of our first meetings that it is absolutely irrelevant which uniform I'm wearing. I'm there as a military representative of NATO and not of a NATO country. That is my understanding of my duty as chairman of the Military Committee, or was my understanding, I should better say. And this regard with respect to these historical issues, I can only repeat once again that in all actions, all counsel which I provided to NATO council - and that is the only the subject here - I did never get any German instruction by no one. I never acted on behalf of Germany. The only thing I did was to act on behalf of the council and the direction which I was given by the NATO council and the NATO Secretary-General. So the question of my German past did not play the slightest role. I would really, Your Honours, for the record, state here I never got any national instruction in the entire Kosovo crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about instructions only, instructions from your country. I'm asking you about a -- I'm asking you as a German general who is familiar with the policy of his country and especially the military aspect. A little while ago, you said that the KLA was considered to be a terrorist organisation, that this was a separatist movement. So that is not being contested; right? Or is that being contested? Is that what you said? Is that what you said? Was that your position?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The -- Your Honours, if I may respond to that. Of course we initially -- and you can read this in NATO statements. Initially we considered the KLA to be -- to act as terrorists, and that is stated, for instance, in the Luxemburg minutes of May 1998. But it would be an absolutely flawed perception if you simply wanted to convey the message that the KLA triggered it all. That is not true. The KLA is to some extent a result of politics which were pursued by your government. It's a result of suppression, of denying of human rights. And you may recall your own role in the Dayton process where it was you who prevented that the issue of Kosovo was discussed or that some of the delegations were of the opinion that one could not find the solution to the Balkan's problem without finding a peaceful solution for Kosovo. So please, Mr. Milosevic, try -- do not try to portray the issue too one-sidedly. You know better than, presumably, I what led to the foundation of the KLA and to the failure of the violence-free process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, please. Are you asserting that Dayton was devoted to Kosovo as well? As far as I can remember, Dayton had to do with peace in Bosnia. That is how it was entitled as well, "General Framework, Peace Agreement on Bosnia." And I imagine that neither you nor I are saying that Kosovo is in Bosnia. So Kosovo was not the subject of any discussions in Dayton, or perhaps is your information different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course Kosovo is not in Bosnia. We are on full agreement on that. And of course the Dayton Agreement does not deal with Kosovo. But you may remember very well in negotiations and in the final phase there was an attempt made by a couple of people to discuss Kosovo and that this attempt failed because you didn't want to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since I asked you about this separatist movement, can you give me an answer to the following: Why the protagonists of the struggle for various separatist projects in the Balkans have a continuity with the fascist allies from the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is precisely the sort of irrelevance which is not going to be allowed. If you persist in asking these questions, Mr. Milosevic, your cross-examination will be brought to an end. Now, you come to some relevant matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that all of this is relevant, but I hope that you won't consider it to be irrelevant if I ask the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you lectured at the Klausewitz Association on the 30th of August 1999 to the elite, you summarised 1999. You said that, "We did not think it would last for 78 days. And without the pictures of refugees in the media, we could not have taken it for more than 78 days." So that is what you said. I am quoting you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness answer. Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it's not being denied that you said this. Yes or no? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I do not deny that. I said this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, let me put a question to you. You are certainly a soldier, and I'm a civilian, so you can give a better answer than this. Is there a war without refugees? Have you ever heard of a war without refugees, as you studied all types of military sciences? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: There was, I think, never a war without refugees, but there is a difference between refugees which flee because of the effects of war and refugees which are driven out of their own -- of their homes and towns by military forces or police forces of the country to which they belong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. A moment ago, towards the end of the examination-in-chief, you said yourself that when the KVM withdrew, violence started. During this violence, after the withdrawal of the KVM, do you include in this violence the NATO bombing and the KLA offensive that carried out mobilisation parallel to the NATO attack on Yugoslavia? Do you include these two elements in violence, or when you refer to violence, are you referring to the violence of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: If you had carefully listened to what I had to say, and provided that the translation was correct, you may have noticed, Mr. Milosevic, that I said that the violence increased when the KVM was withdrawn. That means clearly that there was violence before the KVM was withdrawn, and that is also that violence was there before the NATO bombs were dropped. And I think I said this explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the first reports, the first international reports, recorded flows of refugees only on the 27th of March, on the borders of Macedonia and Albania. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think you have forgotten, and perhaps I may remind you - although you, as the former president of this country, should have known that - that thousands of people had left the country in 1998. They left because forces of your country executed violence in the province of Kosovo. You may also remember that the United Nations refugee relief organisation, the UNHCR, reported that 220.000 citizens of Kosovo, that is, citizens of your country, for which you were responsible, were living outside their villages, towns, and cities in fall 1998, and at this point in time no military action of any foreign country had taken place in your country. So please do not create the image that NATO caused it all. It had begun long before NATO dropped the first bomb, and you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand what you've been saying, that without images of refugees, you could not have taken it for 78 days. Was it the same logic -- and this was the essence of your testimony, just as the essence of the efforts made by this illegal Tribunal, is to justify the aggression of NATO against Yugoslavia and to proclaim that it was Yugoslavia that carried out an aggression against itself, and that everything that happened, all the crimes that occurred, happened because Yugoslavia attacked itself, not because NATO attacked it on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I understand it from the point of view of the accused, but I think the term "aggression" to be used in connotation with NATO's actions is presumably not the understanding of the majority of nations in this world. You may remember, Mr. Milosevic, that a country which definitely is not a part of NATO, namely, Sweden, commissioned an independent inquiry on the Kosovo crisis and came to the conclusion that the NATO air operation was legitimate, although it had a legal deficiency, since it did not have the authorisation of the Security Council. But in this report, which I think is absolutely neutral, the legitimacy of NATO's action is not put into any doubt at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the authority of the United Nations Charter and its obvious violation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going into that now. This is going to be a matter of argument, and no doubt legal argument, in due course. The witness has dealt with what was a very general question. Now, can you ask something particular, and particularly relating to the evidence which he's given, as opposed to these general arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, here, Mr. Naumann, in a special TV show of the ARD Television in Germany - and the authors are two persons, and it was broadcast on the 25th of October, 1999, at 2100 hours - you said, with regard to December 1998, I quote: "In this period, the KLA played an unfortunate role. The KLA saw a vacuum and took advantage of it. It showed in its zones partial territorial sovereignty. In this way, it no doubt provoked the Serb side, and the Serb side reacted just as communist dictators would react, and we see it now in Chechnya as well. If there is a terrorist organisation that crops up, then tanks and artillery are used to attack villages and towns." Now, my question is the following: Is America led by communist dictators in the struggle against terrorism?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to consider whether this cross-examination shouldn't be brought to an end. You have not taken the slightest notice of what you were told and you are abusing the right to cross-examine by these general questions. I'm going to consider the matter with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I not ask the witness even about his own statements on television?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to stop you yet, but you have come very close indeed to having the entire cross-examination stopped. You must understand that the role of cross-examination is to ask the witness questions about his evidence. It's not to try and score political points, which you are doing. If you try and score political points, you'll be stopped. You're abusing the right of cross-examination and you're abusing the process of the Court. So it's a matter for you, Mr. Milosevic, whether this cross-examination continues and how long it's allowed to continue for. But you must understand this, that you've been formally warned that if you continue in this way, it will be brought to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I must say for my own part, I found the General very frank and very candid in the evidence that he gave. For example, he said that he regretted that he was not able to have contact with the KLA, and I found that to be a very frank admission. You might want to ask him whether, as a result of the lack of contact with the KLA, whether the conclusions that he arrived at might have been in any way prejudiced. Well, I'll ask the General himself. General, you said in your examination-in-chief that you were not able to have contact with the KLA, and you conceded that, in your view, it would have been better, in terms of your objective, in terms of what you were trying to do, to achieve, reconciliation and peace, if you were able to have this contact. So it has occurred to me that the conclusions that you arrived at might in some way have been affected by this lack of contact, by the lack of information that would otherwise have been available to you. Would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, with great delight. But first I really should say that I tried to describe the phase between October 25 and December 1998 in a, if I may say so, in a balanced way. I did not accuse one side of being responsible for the outbreak of hostilities and the increase of violence. I tried to convey to you, Your Honours, that both sides contributed to it. And what I had said in that statement Mr. Milosevic quoted a minute ago meant nothing but the fact that the disproportionality, which again and again was applied by the Serb forces, contributed to the escalation, and that, I think, has to be kept in mind. Coming to your question, Your Honour, if we had had a chance to talk to the KLA, we might have been able - but I don't know for sure - we might have been able perhaps to de-escalate. And I said in front of this Court that, with hindsight, I believe we made a mistake by not being allowed to talk to the KLA. Whether this might have resulted in a peaceful solution or not, I simply cannot answer that, Your Honour, since, if I may say so, in all frankness, there are always two to tango, and if one side is not willing to consider peaceful solutions, then all discussions will at the end of the day fail. So I believe there's a lesson learned from the Kosovo involvement. We should really try to do everything to contact all sides concerned, in all future crises, before we resort to the use of military force, since, after all, we are touching upon one of the basic principles of the United Nations Charter, and that is the sovereignty of nations. I'm fully aware - although it has tried to convey that I'm not aware of that - I'm fully aware of Article 2.6 of the United Nations Charter, which clearly forbids intervention. But as a last resort, if everything else had failed, and if there is a risk that thousands of people will be killed, innocent people, or will be expelled, then the international community must have an opportunity to act, and for that reason I dare to say the NATO action was legitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the international community," do you mean the United Nations or do you mean the regional organisation of NATO?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may be aware that NATO is not a regional organisation under the premises of Chapter 8 of the United Nations Charter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. But when you say "the international community," when you use that term, I assume that the institutions which represent the international community - the UN General Assembly, the Security Council - that those are them, and not the NATO committee or council. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course the United Nations are the supreme international authority. They are the only authority which can authorise the use of force. And only in cases - and we had such a case - where the Security Council fails to do its duty and to authorise military action, although the risk of considerable loss of life is imminent, one may come to different conclusions, as did the 16 nations of NATO in the case of the Kosovo intervention. And you should not forget: This was not a decision which came easy for the NATO nations. It was a painful discussion. There were 16 nations which had to take a political decision. In many countries this decision had to be brought to the parliament and had to be agreed upon by 16 - or not in all cases - by a couple of freely elected parliaments. So I think also politically - although I'm, as a military, not here to justify political decisions - I think the political authorities of the NATO countries took the greatest pains possible to come to a balanced conclusion, and as a last resort they authorised the use of force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, another area that you must attend to in your cross-examination is that part of the examination-in-chief where the General attributed certain words to you in a meeting that you had with him and, I believe, Mr. Clark. You were reported to have said, in relation to the Kosovar Albanians, "We will find a solution." And when asked for an explanation --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come to that, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... "same to them as we did in Drenica in 1945 or 1946." "What was that, Mr. President?" "We got them all together and shot them." You must deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come to that, Mr. Robinson. And if you really wish me to, I'll come to it straight away. Actually, I don't know whether even a small child can have any doubts as to the absurdity that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't comment, Mr. Milosevic. You're not here to comment. You're here to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can someone who, five minutes prior to that, signed an agreement, after which, as Mr. Naumann says, everybody felt much easier, said that he has no intention of complying with the agreement but that he would shoot everyone, kill everyone? How can any reasonable being conceive of that? Not only because it would be a crime, but also because it goes against the grain of every assumption as to logic. And Naumann said that finally we have reached an agreement on an issue that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are here to ask questions. You are here to ask questions and not make a speech. I take it from what's being said that this is challenged, and the accused is saying that he did not say this to you. Mr. Naumann, can you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said in my statement, Your Honour, I cross-checked this with the other man who was present and who has exactly the same recollection. And as I also said in a response to your question, Your Honour, we did not comment on that, since we simply couldn't believe it, that anyone could say something like this. So I can only repeat what I have stated. That is my recollection. And as I had said earlier on, I will not say anything but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely because that statement is so unbelievable, how come this astonishing statement on my part, if I gave it, was not used, when the NATO bombing started, in the media campaign which was launched, resorting to all means against Yugoslavia? Why didn't you make use of that statement? But you've just thought about it three years later. You've come up with this absolutely ludicrous statement. How come you didn't publish it anywhere?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I have said this, as has General Clark said, that you made this statement in public long before this day today. And if I recall it properly, it is also mentioned in publications which were published in the United States of America by General Clark. So it's nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, for me this is quite new. I did not expect somebody of your rank to create --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, do you feel now that this is very doubtful from the aspects of material truth, when we bear in mind the fact that what you quoted, what you quoted me as saying about Drenica, was not what happened? Now, do you know -- are you aware of the fact that in the Drenica region, the war of the then Yugoslav army lasted a full two years, with the vestiges of the Balist formations which belonged to the Hitler coalition during the time of the Second World War, and that that struggle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must come to a question. We're not here for speeches. Are you aware of this history which the accused is putting forward, General, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware of, I should say the general lines of that part of history. After our meeting, I tried to dig out facts on this Drenica thing which was not known to me, and in the history books which I have been able to look into so far, I did not find sufficient details for that. But that, I think, is also not relevant since it was just my curiosity which drove me into that type of research to find out what really happened there. Presumably one has to read books which are written in a language which I don't understand and am not able to speak. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In any event, whatever happened is irrelevant as far as this trial is concerned. The issue is whether the accused said it or not. Do you have any doubt that he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, I have no doubts that he did it, and I really cross-examined myself and my memory - which is known throughout, I should say, the German military as being a very good one - again and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, but it is clear to you that what you quoted as having happened in Drenica in 1945 and 1946 and which I allegedly repeated to you, that is to say that we would do the same again, was no kind of gathering up of Albanians and killing Albanians but a continuation of the war with the bands and groups which belonged to the former Hitler units and hid in those hills, and that nobody spoke about Albanians but bands, that nobody had gathered any Albanians in 1945 and 1946 in Drenica to kill them? Are you aware of that fact? Is it something you know about? It is a material -- it is in material opposition to the material facts what you're just saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you putting? Did you say something then about bands being gathered to the generals? Is that what you're saying you told them then, Mr. Milosevic? What is it that you said to them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I am talking about what happened historically at that time, what happened in history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can tell us all about history, insofar as it's relevant, in due course. At the moment, all that is relevant is what it is said that you told the generals. Now, you've asked the general about history, and he's told you what he knows and nothing more, so there's no point going on about that. If you have some alternative case as to what you told them, if you say it was something to do with gathering together bands or something of that sort, then you should put it so that the general can deal with it. Otherwise, I think we have about exhausted this topic. Equally, you should put that you said nothing of the sort, if that is what you claim.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, at all events, and categorically, I did not say that we would gather them and kill them in Drenica, because that would be quite absurd. And I brought up a historical fact to the witness by saying that neither in 1945 or in 1946 did anybody collect Albanians in Drenica to kill them. But in 1945 and 1946, there was still going on with the vestiges of the Hitler army which was made up of Albanian army called the Balist. And now I'm going to add something else which has an even longer history between the First and Second World Wars --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you're not. Now, if there is anything more relevant to this question, you can put it. The general doesn't know anything about the history. You can -- you can tell us about it when it comes to your case. This is what he says that you said to him, and there's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, somebody who knows history, the history of his own country, could not say something like that at all. And that is why I presented this as an argument. It is a material untruth, materially incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the way in which time is wasted, with you arguing all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson has a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... and that's my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is an important issue because it could go to mens rea and other elements that are crucial to the indictment. General, what language was the -- this interview conducted in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you the mean conversation between Mr. Milosevic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Conversation, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was done in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Both General Clark and yourself and the accused spoke English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked a question. General Naumann, do you know that what you're claiming that I said happened in 1945 and 1946 does not correspond to historical truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow this. This is an argument that you are putting the whole time with the witness. The witness knows nothing about the history apart from what he's read in the books. This is what he says that you said. That's the importance of the evidence, whatever the history of it is. Now, he can answer no further, so there's no point going on putting the same question again. Move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The BBC, on the 12th of March, 2000, broadcast a special programme entitled "Moral Combat; NATO at War," which was prepared by Alan Little. In that programme, to make a long story short, I have your quotation in answer to his question, which was: "Ambassador Walker, in the NATO council, presented the fact that peace was generally being violated by the KLA." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: If you have the quotation of the BBC, I said it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I can't recall it at the moment, but I would like to make one point, Mr. Milosevic. I said in my evidence, and you may have heard that, that in the phase between beginning of November 1998 and December 1998, the majority of incidents was triggered, to the best of my knowledge, by the KLA. But I also stated that the response by the Serb security forces was again and again characterised by disproportionate force -- use of force. And that, I think, explains what I said and what I used as quotation of Ambassador Walker to which you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware, Mr. Naumann, how many people were killed, citizens in Kosovo, by the KLA, both Serbs and Albanians and Turks and Romas? How many policemen were killed, how many soldiers, throughout that time, prior to your intervention? And are you bearing all this in mind when you're talking about the disproportionate or proportionate use of force?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, I bear that in mind. And I think I said also in my written evidence which is in front of this Court that I have spoken to German police officers who were serving in Kosovo, who reported to me that KLA/UCK elements really misbehaved grossly in killing and torturing Serb police officers. And that is simply intolerable. On that point I think we are in full agreement. But one should never forget, first of all, how did it all come about; and secondly, who was in control of the spiral of escalation which later on led to a conflict for which we saw no other resolution. And please don't forget, if you talk about the victims on the side of the Serbs, that there were hundreds and thousands of people in Kosovo, citizens of your country, who lost their life because of the action of your security forces. And it started all in this escalation in spring 1998, and you are -- I think you're aware of that. So don't try to -- to establish a balance which I think at the end of the day will not play in your favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, did I hear you properly? Did you say that hundreds of thousands of citizens lost their lives in Kosovo? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I said hundreds or thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Hundreds or thousands, or thousands, of citizens. Well, that's what I'm talking about precisely. Now, I'm precisely talking about that. Several thousands lost their lives in the war, several thousands in the war. Serbs died, Albanians, Turks. Romas died. War is a crime, but as far as I'm able to understand, that war was launched by the NATO pact, Mr. Naumann, is that correct or not, the war against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, according to the statements of your own authorities, approximately 500 civilians of your country were killed during the NATO air operation, and a couple of hundred military personnel. That, I think, is what was done. I do not hesitate to say that any innocent civilian who lost his life, regardless of which nationality, is one too much.
