By I also really dare to say, with good confidence, that we took the utmost pain to avoid casualties among the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's move on, and I hope we will be a bit more dynamic. But did I understand you correctly? The figures you've just quoted, as far as I was able to understand, they refer to the ones that you killed from the air, the people you killed from the air.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement for the Senate Armed Service Committee in Washington on the 3rd of November, 1999, you said that the most important thing was, as you say, to question the myth that ethnic cleansing only began after the start of the bombing; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I said that. You have it in writing, presumably, in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, you are endeavouring in every way possible to justify the NATO aggression by saying that the fact of the mass exodus, the mass exodus took place after the bombing, you're trying to challenge that and question it and to make it seem that it all began much earlier and that the exodus of the civilians was not the result of the bombing but, rather, the result of some sort of violence on the part of the Serb forces. Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Mr. Milosevic, and I don't know how often --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. Let him explain.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: -- how often I have to repeat that 220.000 citizens of your country were living under miserable conditions in October 1998, somewhere in the forests of Kosovo, because they were driven out from their homes by your security forces. So the exodus began before the first bomb was dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, are you aware of the fact that people fled just from the areas where the KLA was waging struggles against the police and army? Do you know about that, that quite simply the citizens wanted to get away from an area in which there was shooting? The internally displaced persons would go to another village where they had relatives if there was shooting going on in their own village. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, I think that's one way to put it. I have heard other witnesses saying that they simply fled because security forces, police or someone else, or militia, simply drove them out of their homes, burned their homes and the villages, and they had nowhere to go but to live somewhere in the forest. And by the way, we took some aerial photographs of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And tell me this: How do you explain, in view of the proportions of the population and all the rest of it, why, then, if the refugees are the consequence of other reasons and not the NATO bombing, why, then, did 100.000 Serbs, during the bombing, flee from Kosovo? Who were they fleeing from then?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, I think some of them may have left their homes because of fear of NATO attacks. On the other hand, I think you will agree that NATO took really great pain to avoid the bombing of housing areas and things like this. We strictly targeted military targets. And that was also checked by international authorities, and they -- they agreed in their findings that NATO's rules of engagement were very strict and in full compliance with international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you say that you strictly targeted military targets, I wish to ask you the following: Here, for example, it is the front line that I have, and I'm quoting you, the question was: "Could I ask you it terms of authorisation of airstrikes what was the most difficult target or set of targets you had to authorise?" [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ...was the thing that sticks in your mind? [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ...I think difficult things was to really go for the first target in downtown Belgrade. We had -- General Clark asked us, the Secretary-General and myself, to authorise a strike against the police headquarters, Ministry of Interior..." [Interpretation] and so on. And you say that there was a hospital close by and that great care had to be taken that the hospital should not be hit. Of course, the hospital was hit. Now, I am asking you, in view of the fact that you say that Clark asked you and the Secretary-General -- now, did you, the Secretary-General and Clark, were you the body, the authority, which authorised the targets to be bombed?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I mentioned that example in one statement in public to indicate that we really took the utmost care in targeting areas even in downtown Belgrade. And General Clark had not been given the authority to target downtown Belgrade without special political permission, and to that ended to go to the Secretary-General. And he provided us with aerial photography of the target. That the MUP headquarters was a target which was targetable under international law is without any doubt, but unfortunately, we had this hospital right next to it. And I saw it on the aerial photography, and we asked General Clark to go back and to recalculate the targeting of this specific target in such a way that he could guarantee us with the utmost certainty that not a single window would be broken in the hospital. He came back. He assured us that this would be possible, and then the Secretary-General authorised this target. And on the very next day, we saw on the aerial photography, and we heard it also by your own media, that indeed not a single glass was broken in that hospital. It was absolutely unharmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And who authorised the destruction of the mining centre in Aleksinac and the mining town of Aleksinac with a civilian character and where there were no military installations? The bombing of Aleksinac, a mining town in the centre, in the heart of Serbia where the population is poor. Poor people live there. So their houses, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm -- I really do not know every single target since it was not the task of the Military Committee to overlook every single target. What we did was to authorise, let's say, the general rules of engagement and to set the limits for the executing Supreme Allied Commander, and we closely watched to which extent he really remained within the limits. And I can report to the Court that SACEUR really scrupulously remained within the authorised limits. There were exceptions or there were -- there were stray bombs, as you know. But again I should say, so that we put the record straight, of the approximately 28.000 munitions which were dropped throughout these 78 days of the air campaign, 1 per cent failed, to some extent due to hostile anti-aircraft fire, to some extent due to technical failures or pilot errors. But that, I think, has to be said as well. And again I say if there were civilian casualties -- if there is one civilian casualty, Mr. Milosevic, it's one too much. But we did --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to bring this to an end. The time has now come. It's after 4.00. There is another matter to attend to. We will continue in the morning. General, would you be back please tomorrow morning at 9.00 to conclude your evidence. Mr. Milosevic, we've considered how long you should have and nature and manner of the cross-examination so far. We've borne in mind the significance of the evidence. We've come to the conclusion that you will have two hours more in the morning, so you should prepare your examination accordingly. General, if you would like to retire now. We've got some other matter to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of June, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.05 p.m.,
